notes.text: Then Peter standing up — All the gestures, all the words of Peter, show the utmost sobriety; lifted up his voice - With cheerfulness and boldness; and said to them - This discourse has three parts; each of which, ver. 14, 22, 29, begins with the same appellation, men: only to the last part he prefixes with more familiarity the additional word brethren. Men of Judea - That is, ye that are born in Judea. St. Peter spoke in Hebrew, which they all understood.

glossa.text: *Jewish men.* That is, there are two causes of prudence, namely that they were Jews, and that they dwelt in Jerusalem, which sobriety becomes.

notes.text: The sorrows — Dangerous and deadly calamities. Pains - Such agonies and horrors, as dying persons use to feel.

glossa.text:
*I have loved.* ((ID.)) This the sheep says which had strayed, the son returned, the pilgrim of this world.

((CASS.)) *I have loved.* Not for the temporal goods given to me, as the unbelievers do, but *because,* etc. God is loved even by unbelievers because he gives good things; whence: *I will praise thee when thou shalt do well to him ((Psal. XLVIII))*. He is loved perfectly, him *eum*; read *cum*, "when" the mind is not moved by adverse things, but is kindled by hope: which manner he afterwards expounds, *I have loved.* Not because he made me a king, or gave me prosperity, but because he hears my prayer in straits.

*And in my days.* ((AUG.)) Namely of my misery, which days I made for myself by sinning, which are full of labour and sorrow, that is, of the old rottenness.

*I will call upon.* Which is not without faith; whence the Apostle: *How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? ((Rom. X.))* When therefore he says, *they shall call upon,* note that the lover is not idle. In which, *They have compassed me,* etc. Or, in the days of salvation, that is, in the time of fulness; whence: *Behold, now is the acceptable time,* etc. ((II Cor. VI)).

*Sorrows.* ((CASS.)) Sins, whence come the sorrow and the death of the soul; or eternal sorrows, and this shall be in hell. *The perils of hell.* ((AUG.)) For, steeped in carnal pleasure, I did not perceive the evils that compassed me about.
*Trouble and sorrow.* ((ID.)) As it were: those things first compassed me about, but afterwards I found trouble and sorrow, that is, outward affliction, to be profitable.

notes.text: Who judgeth according to every man's work — According to the tenor of his life and conversation. Pass the time of your sojourning - Your short abode on earth. In humble, loving fear - The proper companion and guard of hope.
Your vain conversation — Your foolish, sinful way of life.
Without blemish — In himself. Without spot - From the world.

Who through him believe — For all our faith and hope proceed from the power of his resurrection. In God that raised Jesus, and gave him glory - At his ascension. Without Christ we should only dread God; whereas through him we believe, hope, and love.

Having purified your souls by obeying the truth through the Spirit, who bestows upon you freely, both obedience and purity of heart, and unfeigned love of the brethren, go on to still higher degrees of love. Love one another fervently — With the most strong and tender affection; and yet with a pure heart - Pure from any spot of unholy desire or inordinate passion.
Which liveth — Is full of divine virtue. And abideth the same forever.

glossa.text:
*In fear,* etc. ((HIER.)) I, defiled with all the filth of sins, day and night await with trembling to pay the last farthing. And the time when it shall be said to me, Jerome, come forth.

*Of your sojourning.* That you may be able to be holy, have your conversation in fear, in the time of your sojourning, so long as you are in the exile of this world. *For blessed is he that is always fearful,* this I say if you call upon God, as if he should say: You do not truly call upon God, unless you be solicitous and fearful.

*But with the precious blood.* The order of the letter is: but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb uncontaminated and unspotted. Here he touches upon the Levitical and priestly celebrations. And he signifies the clean soul, through justice, which is offered to God.

notes.text: Mark xvi, 12.
Today is the third day — The day he should have risen again, if at all.
O foolish — Not understanding the designs and works of God: And slow of heart - Unready to believe what the prophets have so largely spoken.

Ought not Christ — If he would redeem man, and fulfil the prophecies concerning him, to have suffered these things? - These very sufferings which occasion your doubts, are the proofs of his being the Messiah. And to enter into his glory - Which could be done no other way.
He made as though he would go farther — Walking forward, as if he was going on; and he would have done it, had they not pressed him to stay.
They constrained him — By their importunate entreaties.
He took the bread, and blessed, and brake — Just in the same manner as when he instituted his last supper.
Their eyes were opened — That is, the supernatural cloud was removed: And he vanished - Went away insensibly.
Did not our heart burn within us — Did not we feel an unusual warmth of love! Was not our heart burning, &c.
The same hour — Late as it was.

The Lord hath appeared to Simon — Before he was seen of the twelve apostles, 1 Cor. xv, 5. He had, in his wonderful condescension and grace, taken an opportunity on the former part of that day (though where, or in what manner, is not recorded) to show himself to Peter, that he might early relieve his distresses and fears, on account of having so shamefully denied his Master.
In the breaking of bread — The Lord's Supper.

glossa.text: *Named Emmaus.* Emmaus is itself the metropolis, a notable city of Palestine, which, after the storming of Judea, was restored under the prince Marcus Aurelius Antonius, and changed its name along with its condition.

*While they talked together.* The Lord draws near and accompanies them as they speak of him, that he may both kindle in their minds the faith of the resurrection, and fulfil what he had promised he would do: *Where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them ((Matth. XXVIII))*. *Drawing near,* etc. *Their eyes,* etc. He appeared indeed in his own form, but did not show the form which they might recognize. As they both loved him within and yet doubted, so he himself is present outside and at hand, and does not show who he is. To those who speak of him, then, he grants his presence; but from those who doubt of him he takes away the appearance by which he might be known.

*Art thou a stranger,* etc. *To whom,* etc. They think him a stranger whom they do not recognize. And truly he was a stranger to them, from whose frailty he now stood far off through the glory of the resurrection, and from whose faith, ignorant of the resurrection, he remained an alien. *A man, a prophet,* etc. *And how they delivered him up,* etc. They confess him a prophet and a great one; of the Son of God they are silent, either because they do not yet believe perfectly, or, if they believe, they fear to be delivered into the hands of the Jews, not knowing with whom they speak.

*But we hoped,* etc. In a manner they refute themselves, in that they had hoped for redemption in him whom they had seen dead, nor did they believe that he would rise again; and they grieve most of all that he was slain without guilt, whom they had known to be innocent; and from this they were walking sorrowful .

*They affrighted us,* etc. They are rightly said *teruisse* those to whom they added more sadness about the body not found than they bring gladness, by the resurrection announced, wherewith they might be refreshed.

*Some of us went,* etc. Since above he said that Peter ran to the monument, and now Cleophas says: *Some of us went to the monument,* etc., it is to be understood that two went together. But he mentioned Peter alone first, because Mary announced it to him first.

*O foolish and slow of heart.* Here a twofold necessity of being humbled presses upon us, who are neither taught in the Scriptures as much as we ought, nor as intent as is fitting on fulfilling the things we know. For if Moses and the prophets spoke of Christ, and had foretold that he would enter through passion into glory, how does he glory that he is a Christian who neither searches out in the Scriptures how they pertain to Christ, nor desires to reach through sufferings the glory which he wishes to have with Christ?

*And he himself,* etc. *Stay with us,* etc. He showed himself such in body as he was among them in mind. They were to be tested, whether they would love at least as a stranger him whom they did not yet love as God. But because they cannot be strangers to the brightness, they with whom the Truth was walking call him to lodging, nay compel him. From which example it is gathered that strangers are not only to be invited to lodging, but even to be drawn in.

*He broke it,* etc. Him whom they did not know in the exposition of Scripture they knew in the breaking of bread; because not the hearers of the law but the doers shall be justified, and the truth is better understood by working than by hearing.
*Their eyes were opened,* etc. The appearance of weakness is withdrawn from the eyes of the flesh, that the glory of the resurrection may begin to appear to their minds.

*And they said,* etc. Mystically: for this reason another likeness was shown them in Christ, that they might not know him save in the breaking of bread; so that all may understand that they do not recognize Christ unless they become partakers of his body, that is, of the Church, whose unity the Apostle commends in the sacrament of the bread, saying: *We being many are one bread, one body ((I Cor. X))*. When therefore he reaches out the blessed bread, their eyes are opened that they may know him, and the impediment is removed which was upon their eyes from Satan, that Jesus might not be recognized. And this impediment the Lord allows to remain until the sacrament of the bread be come to. But when the unity of the body has been shared, the enemy's impediment is taken away, that Christ may be recognized.

*Burning. ((GREG.))* When the word had been heard, the heart, before cold with the numbness of unbelief and of fear, was kindled with the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that it now burns with a heavenly desire and stretches itself out to believe the truth. By as many precepts as a man is instructed, by so many torches, as it were, is he set aflame.

*The Lord is risen.* Already there was a report that Jesus had risen, made by those women and by Simon Peter, to whom he had appeared; these two found them speaking of these things. But they themselves also had heard earlier that he had risen; yet they feared to say it on the way, when they said only that angels had been seen by the women. For, not knowing him with whom they were speaking, they could fear that they might fall into the hands of the Jews, if they should say anything anywhere about Christ's resurrection.

registers.label: Spare
lines: We walked away from the city, slow with grief.
He came alongside and would not leave us.
At the table he took the bread and broke it.
Our eyes were opened, and we knew him.
What can we give for all his goodness to us?
We will lift the cup of salvation.
Christ is risen!
Christ is risen, alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: You who set out this morning heavy-hearted, with hope gone cold behind you — come and sit, for the road is not the end of the story.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
Watch his hands take the loaf, bless it, break it; the same hands that were pierced now passing you the bread.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
And there, in the breaking, the stranger is no stranger, and the grief becomes a fire that sends us running back.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
What shall we render for such goodness? We lift the cup of salvation and call upon his name.
Christ is risen, alleluia!
